name: Baconian fallacy
statement: The idea that a researcher can gather facts without a question to select them, and reach a general truth by piling them up.
meaning: Fischer's definition is that the fallacy "consists in the idea that a historian can operate without the aid of preconceived questions, hypotheses, ideas, assumptions, theories, paradigms, postulates, prejudices, presumptions, or general presuppositions of any kind". The historian is then "supposed to go a-wandering in the dark forest of the past, gathering facts like nuts and berries, until he has enough to make a general truth". Fischer calls the idea doubly deficient, because it sets an impossible object and an impracticable method. The method fails because there is no practicable limit to the number of true statements about the past. He quotes Quine: "Truths are as plentiful as falsehoods, since each falsehood admits of a negation which is true." The object fails because the whole truth is not available, in any of the three forms Fischer says the quest takes. A historian, he writes, "can only hope to know something about something". This is a charge about how an inquiry is organised, not a measurement of a mind.

origin.where: Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought
origin.note: The section opens chapter I, "Fallacies of Question-Framing", and runs from page 4 to page 8 of the Harper edition. Both of the book's indexes list it at 4-8. Fischer did not coin the name and says so. His footnote takes it from Francis Bacon's account of a method which "derives its axioms from the senses and particulares, rising by a gradual and unbroken ascent, so that it arrives at the most general axioms last of all". The citation is Novum Organum book I, aphorism xix. Fischer then adds that "this is unfair to Bacon, and inaccurate as an understanding of his thought". He keeps the name only "because it is standard", quoting H. W. B. Joseph's remark that "if it is useful to have a nomenclature of fallacies, it is useful to have a standard nomenclature".

evidence:
The book argues by specimen, and in these five pages there is no experiment, no sample and no rate. The clearest specimen is not Bacon. Fischer writes that "the best and clearest illustration is not Bacon, or Ranke, but a distinguished French historian, Fustel de Coulanges". He quotes Fustel telling a historian to "carefully observe all the facts, all the institutions, all regulations public or private, all the customs of domestic life", because "he does not know beforehand from which side enlightenment will come to him". Fischer's rebuttal is biographical rather than statistical. On G. P. Gooch's report Fustel "regarded his results as independent of himself and felt criticism as something like blasphemy". Fischer says the nationalist bias Fustel thought he had removed was merely disguised. It surfaced as a minimisation of Teutonic influence, in a work written just after the Franco-Prussian war. Four lighter specimens follow. Samuel Eliot Morison distinguishes the "realm of hypothesis" from "the realm of history". G. R. Elton writes that the historian "becomes the servant of his evidence of which he will, or should, ask no specific questions until he has absorbed what it says". The other two are Dr Johnson's opinion that "questioning is not a mode of conversation among gentlemen", and Kipling's "them that asks no questions, isn't told a lie". Fischer's positive case is the New Economic Historians, whom he names as making their questions and models explicit. The chapter closes with six axioms, of which the second matters most here: a question "should be open-ended, but not wide-open". Fischer announces "ten fallacies of empirical question-framing" at the start of the chapter and calls them "these eleven common fallacies" at the end. Eleven is the number that can be counted in the text.

Bacon's own text does not describe the method the name attributes to him. Aphorism xix of book I sets out two ways of investigating truth and prefers the one that "constructs its axioms from the senses and particulars, by ascending continually and gradually". Aphorism civ says the understanding must not be allowed to "jump and fly from particulars to remote and most general axioms", and that "we must not then add wings, but rather lead and ballast to the understanding". Aphorism cv is the sentence that matters: "The induction which proceeds by simple enumeration is puerile, leads to uncertain conclusions, and is exposed to danger from one contradictory instance, deciding generally from too small a number of facts, and those only the most obvious." What Bacon wants instead is a procedure that separates nature "by proper rejections and exclusions". The tables in book II are not an undirected collection. They begin "a nature being given", and the worked example is the form of heat: a table of instances agreeing in heat, a table of proximate instances wanting it, and a table of degrees. The negatives are chosen for their closeness to the positives, because "if, however, we were to examine every instance, our labor would be infinite", which is Fischer's own objection to the fallacy that carries Bacon's name. Joseph, the logician Fischer cites for the nomenclature, reads Bacon's induction as a disjunctive argument in which alternative hypotheses about the form are eliminated by the facts. Bacon's word for reasoning applied to nature ahead of the evidence is "anticipation", and he sets it against "interpretation"; the caricature reads the second term as a ban on questions rather than a ban on premature answers.

replication.headline: No study was found that measures the Baconian fallacy, in historians or in anyone else. The nearest measured thing is what happens when a data set is analysed without a question, and those results cut in both directions.
replication.detail:
Europe PMC holds no record containing the phrase "Baconian fallacy". Crossref returns nothing under it either; its bibliographic query degrades to loose matching and offers an 1844 volume called A Discourse of the Baconian Philosophy and an Oxford English Dictionary entry for the adjective. Nothing located scores historical writing for the error or gives it a rate.

The closest formal statement of Fischer's claim is Ioannidis's third corollary: "the greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true". His table 4 puts a figure on it. For discovery-oriented exploratory research with massive testing, where tested relationships outnumber true ones a thousandfold, power is 0.20 and bias is 0.80, the positive predictive value comes out at 0.0010, rising to 0.0015 when bias is held to 0.20. Those are values of an algebraic model under assumed parameters, not counts of anything observed.

What has been observed is the spread that appears when one data set is analysed every defensible way. Wang and colleagues took 70 analytic methods from 15 published studies of red meat and mortality and applied 1,208 of them to 10,661 NHANES participants. Hazard ratios ran on both sides of 1, with 435 specifications at or above it and 773 below, a median of 0.94 and an interquartile range of 0.83 to 1.05. Forty-eight, or 3.97%, reached statistical significance, 40 pointing one way and eight the other. Tierney and colleagues ran the same kind of check on 581 microbe-disease associations already reported in the literature, across 15 cohorts and 2,343 individuals. One taxon in three showed substantial inconsistency in the sign of the association. More than 90% of published type 1 and type 2 diabetes findings were among the unstable.

The evidence also runs the other way, which is why this entry does not treat Fischer's charge as confirmed. Border and colleagues identified 18 depression candidate genes, each studied ten or more times between 1991 and 2016, and tested them in samples ranging from 62,138 to 443,264. No clear evidence appeared for any polymorphism association or any polymorphism-by-environment effect, and as a set the candidate genes were no more associated with depression than noncandidate genes. Those were the facts a question had selected. The genome-wide scans that select nothing by hypothesis are the ones whose results have held. Numbers on analytic flexibility as a researcher's choice, rather than as a property of a question-free design, are on this site's garden-of-forking-paths and Texas sharpshooter entries rather than repeated here.

limits:
The search for a measurement covered Europe PMC by phrase, Crossref by bibliographic query and general web search. No psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched, and JSTOR was not searched. Whether the phrase "Baconian fallacy" was in print before 1970 was not settled. Fischer says the name is standard and cites Joseph only for the principle of standard nomenclature. The string "Baconian" does not occur in Joseph's 1906 Introduction to Logic, whose Internet Archive text was searched in full in two renderings. Google Books returned a daily quota error on every attempt and HathiTrust full-text search returned a bot check. The Internet Archive full-text index returned no hits for a phrase that is certainly in one of its own books. All three of those searches failed rather than came up empty.

Fischer's text was read as two independent renderings of the same Internet Archive scan, the plain text and an extraction from the PDF, and every quotation above was checked in both. Novum Organum was read in Joseph Devey's translation at Project Gutenberg, as plain text and again as HTML. Fischer quotes aphorism xix in a different translation, so the wording in the origin note and the wording in the evidence section differ; both were read, and the Latin was not consulted. The three books Fischer cites for the claim that Bacon was misread, by Farrington, Anderson and Fussner, were not obtained. Neither was Fustel de Coulanges's Histoire des Institutions Politiques, nor Gooch, nor Elton, so those quotations reach this page through Fischer.

Ioannidis's table 4 was read in the PLOS manuscript XML and again in the article PDF; the Europe PMC rendering carries the table as an image and its figures could not be read there. Border and colleagues' abstract figures were read at PubMed and again in the author manuscript at PubMed Central. The manuscript's further numbers, including the total N of 621,214 and the power calculation, rest on a single file and are not quoted here. Two attempts to obtain a PDF of that manuscript were refused. Wikipedia's API was rate-limited throughout, so its article on Historians' Fallacies was read once and its coverage of this fallacy was not established.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to read the name as Fischer's verdict on Francis Bacon. The footnote that introduces the name says the opposite. The attribution is "unfair to Bacon, and inaccurate as an understanding of his thought", because Bacon's larger work "did not defend an induction as simple-minded as this, but rather a more complex method of interdependent inquiry and research". Fischer's line for it is that "Bacon was no more a Baconian than Marx was a Marxian, or Plato a Platonist". Two pages later he adds that the best illustration is not Bacon. Bacon appears in the book's index at three page numbers and is a specimen at none of them.

The second error is to assume that Bacon's tables of instances are the fact-gathering the fallacy describes. They are not. Book II sets them out for a given nature, the worked case being heat, and the negative instances are restricted to what stands close to the positives on the express ground that examining every instance would take infinite labour. Bacon calls induction by simple enumeration puerile. A reader who wants the position Fischer attacks should look at the Fustel de Coulanges passage Fischer quotes, which does tell a historian to bring no question at all.

A third is to take the fallacy as a general result that hypothesis-free inquiry finds less. In psychiatric genetics it went the other way. Border and colleagues tested 18 candidate genes chosen by hypotheses about the biology of depression, in samples up to 443,264, and found no clear evidence for any of them. The agnostic genome scan is the design that survived.

A fourth is to expect an effect size. There is none, because the claim is about the structure of an inquiry rather than about a tendency that has been given to volunteers. A fifth is to read Fischer as demanding that the question be settled before the evidence is seen. His second axiom asks for a question that is "open-ended, but not wide-open", one that "should dictate the kinds of facts which will serve to solve a problem, without dictating the solution itself". His method for holding the two together is to start with a cluster of questions and rival hypotheses, designed "to neutralize a predisposition to actualize any one of them".

sources.text: Fischer, D. H. (1970). Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought. New York: Harper & Row. Pages 4 to 8 read in full for the definition, footnote 2, the Quine and Huizinga quotations and the Fustel, Morison, Elton, Johnson and Kipling specimens; pages 38 to 39 for the six affirmative axioms; the two indexes for the locators. Read as the Internet Archive scan, both the plain text and an extraction from the PDF of the same item, with every quotation checked in both.

Bacon, F. Novum Organum, translated and edited by Joseph Devey (New York: P. F. Collier, 1902). Book I aphorisms xix, xxvi, civ and cv, and book II aphorisms x to xx, read for the two ways of investigating truth, anticipation against interpretation, the ballast on the understanding, simple enumeration as puerile, and the three tables and first vintage of the form of heat. Read at Project Gutenberg as plain text and again as HTML.

Joseph, H. W. B. (1906). An Introduction to Logic. Oxford: Clarendon Press. The appendix on fallacies read for the standard-nomenclature sentence Fischer quotes from page 533, and the chapter on induction read for Joseph's reading of Bacon's method as a disjunctive elimination of alternative hypotheses. Read as the Internet Archive plain text and again as the item's hOCR search text; the string "Baconian" occurs in neither.

Ioannidis, J. P. A. (2005). Why most published research findings are false. PLoS Medicine, 2(8), e124. Source for corollary 3 and for the table 4 positive predictive values of 0.0010 and 0.0015 for discovery-oriented exploratory research with massive testing. Read as the PLOS manuscript XML and again in the article PDF, because the Europe PMC copy carries table 4 as an image.

Wang, Y., Pitre, T., Wallach, J. D., de Souza, R. J., Jassal, T., Bier, D., Patel, C. J., & Zeraatkar, D. (2024). Grilling the data: application of specification curve analysis to red meat and all-cause mortality. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 168, 111278. Full text read at Europe PMC and the figures confirmed against the PubMed abstract.

Tierney, B. T., Tan, Y., Yang, Z., Shui, B., Walker, M. J., Kent, B. M., Kostic, A. D., & Patel, C. J. (2022). Systematically assessing microbiome-disease associations identifies drivers of inconsistency in metagenomic research. PLOS Biology, 20(3), e3001556. Full text read at Europe PMC and the figures confirmed against the PubMed abstract.

Border, R., Johnson, E. C., Evans, L. M., Smolen, A., Berley, N., Sullivan, P. F., & Keller, M. C. (2019). No support for historical candidate gene or candidate gene-by-interaction hypotheses for major depression across multiple large samples. American Journal of Psychiatry, 176(5), 376-387. Abstract read at PubMed and again in the author manuscript at PubMed Central; only the abstract's figures are used here.
